articles.title: America's reddest state chases billion-dollar boom as others sour on massive emerging industry
articles.summary: Wyoming's vast land, affordable energy and fiber optic corridors could lure billions in data center investment as other states add new taxes.
articles.body: As Americans weigh the costs and benefits of massive data centers emerging in their towns to fuel the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, the country's reddest state could be poised to capitalize on billions of dollars in investment that other states are increasingly reluctant to welcome. With wide-open spaces, abundant energy and a business-friendly environment, Wyoming has many of the ingredients tech companies are looking for as they race to expand their AI infrastructure in the U.S. The opportunity comes as the rapid buildout of data centers has sparked political fights across the country over their enormous electricity demands, water use and tax treatment. As some states and communities consider new taxes, restrictions or even moratoriums on data center construction, Wyoming has a chance to position itself as an alternative. Supporters argue the projects could bring billions of dollars onto local tax rolls and potentially ease the burden on homeowners. THIS TINY FARMING TOWN YOU’VE NEVER HEARD OF IS HELPING MICROSOFT SELL AMERICA ON DATA CENTERS And Wyoming already checks many of the boxes data center developers are looking for. "Data centers need a few things. They need land, they need affordable energy, they need to avoid natural disasters, and, of course, they need regulatory approval," Jared Walczak, vice president of state projects at the Tax Foundation, told Fox News Digital. The Cowboy State also already has high-capacity fiber running along major interstate corridors, Walczak said, giving developers another key piece of infrastructure. "If more states start imposing discriminatory taxes just on data centers, then places like Wyoming, at least as long as they don't do likewise, can become even more attractive," he said. ONE OF THE WORLD'S HOTTEST INDUSTRIES IS SPARKING A BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM Wyoming is wrestling with some of the same questions confronting communities elsewhere. Cheyenne officials rejected a proposed one-year moratorium on new data centers in May following public debate over electricity rates, water use and other concerns. Wyoming lawmakers have also considered reclassifying data centers as industrial property, a move that would subject them to a higher property tax assessment rate. ELECTION WHISTLEBLOWER WARNS FOREIGN ACTORS ARE SPENDING BILLIONS TO TURN AMERICANS AGAINST AI But Walczak argues that attracting the facilities could deliver a significant payoff for Wyoming homeowners. "You have potentially billions of dollars worth of taxable property coming into a couple hundred acres," he said. "And that's the sort of increase in the tax base that can allow significant property tax relief for every other payer in the jurisdiction." "Wyoming's been having a lot of conversations about lowering property taxes," Walczak added. "This is a great way to do that." He pointed to Loudoun County, Virginia, the country’s largest data center market, as an example of how that tax base can benefit residents. "Data centers provide about 45% of all local tax revenue to Loudoun County," Walczak said, adding that the average homeowner would pay an estimated $5,800 more annually in property taxes without the industry. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The economic upside comes with a broader debate over who pays for the infrastructure needed to serve the power-hungry facilities. Walczak said data centers can avoid pushing those costs onto residents if operators pay for the additional generation and transmission capacity they require. For Wyoming, that leaves policymakers facing the same question confronting states nationwide as they look to capture a piece of the AI investment boom without leaving residents to shoulder the costs.

articles.title: 9/11 Museum unveils exhibition for generation too young to remember the attacks: 'Called everybody to lead'
articles.summary: The 9/11 Memorial and Museum unveils a new exhibition featuring artifacts and firsthand accounts showing how the attacks inspired a generation of service.
articles.body: The 9/11 Memorial and Museum is marking the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks by unveiling a new exhibition exploring the legacy of service inspired by that day and preserving its history for the next generation. In Their Honor: 25 Years of 9/11 Inspired Service highlights how 9/11 inspired thousands of Americans to serve their communities and country in the years that followed. "So many people who visit the museum or who are interested in learning about 9/11 are too young to remember themselves, and one of the stories that they don't necessarily realize when they start to encounter the history of 9/11 is how much it changed the arc of people's lives," 9/11 Memorial and Museum President and CEO Elizabeth L. Hillman told Fox News Digital. The exhibition features artifacts, interactive displays, and firsthand accounts from those who turned the tragedy into a lifetime of service, including military members, first responders, volunteers, educators and victims' families. AMERICA’S HEARTLAND COMES FACE-TO-FACE WITH 9/11 HISTORY AS 25TH ANNIVERSARY NEARS Hillman said the exhibition's "signature artifact" is Feathers of the Phoenix , a 15-foot papier-mâché sculpture created by children who lost loved ones on 9/11 while attending America's Camp. "The reason I think that's the best artifact to talk about the entire exhibition is that those young people have grown up, and the exhibition is about what they decided to do in the wake of that loss they suffered on 9/11," she said. Outside the exhibition, the museum also offers a free digital learning experience with a 35-minute film featuring six personal stories. One story follows brothers James and Patrick Dowdell, whose firefighter father was killed responding to the Sept. 11 attacks, inspiring James to join the Fire Department of New York and Patrick to serve in the U.S. Army. "I think that first-person storytelling is the way to reach young people," Hillman said. MASSIVE PIECE OF 9/11 HISTORY MAKES STUNNING 10,500-MILE JOURNEY ACROSS AMERICA With more children growing up with no memory of 9/11, Hillman said the museum tailors its educational resources by age and recommends tools like "Sesame Street's" post-9/11 episodes to help families discuss the attacks. "There are age-appropriate materials that change over time for what students are ready to understand," she said. Hillman said the museum is preparing the next generation to carry forward the lessons. "We need to reach the people who are becoming teachers, who are becoming firefighters, police officers, members of the Armed Forces, and help them understand what it was to come together after 9/11 and develop a response to a catastrophe that we did not anticipate," she said. WHERE TUNNEL TO TOWERS' STEEL ACROSS AMERICA TOUR WILL STOP AHEAD OF 9/11 Twenty-five years later, Hillman said the museum's mission is more important than ever. "It really called everybody to lead," she said. "I think that's different now than what it has been at previous points in time when we were closer to the attacks and not 25 years away." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The exhibition opens to the public on Sept. 12.

articles.title: In Ukraine, Putin is running out of time and options
articles.summary: Putin is all-in, and he will escalate to achieve his desired end state, because the alternative is his own demise.
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin’s special military operation in Ukraine was supposed to succeed within a week or two. It has now dragged on for 1,659 days, and the Russian machine only has so much patience.

Last week The Economist suggested that Putin believes that ending the war short of success “would put him physically at risk.”

“They will hang me,” he is said to have confessed to cronies earlier in the war.

He is running out of time for winning, and out of options. But he does still have options.

His first option — the least intrusive — is to stay on the current path. He wants to persuade President Trump to force Ukraine into a peace deal on his terms — a deal that eliminates what he claims were the root causes for the war.

Last weekend, he hosted U.S. Envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner in Moscow. The two were met on the tarmac by Putin’s economic envoy, Kirill Dmitriev. The same Dmitriev who pitched them a $14 trillion joint project in February, contingent upon a peace agreement in Ukraine and the lifting of Western sanctions.

But peace required Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to cede the Donbas to Russia, and Trump cannot deliver that.

On Tuesday, Putin spoke with Trump for an hour. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov described the conversation as constructive, and that Trump believed ending the war would open up “impressive and far-reaching” prospects for fully restoring relations between Washington and Moscow, and that “this would have a particular impact on trade and economic ties, promising enormous benefits for both countries.”

It is the same message eight months later. Economic deals are still on the table — hence Dmitriev’s presence at the airport.

Putin’s second option involves pressuring NATO and the European Union into withdrawing their support to Ukraine by threatening to expand the war beyond Ukraine’s border. The Kremlin is doing that now through a hybrid warfare campaign , demonstrations of military force, and threats to attack countries providing military support and technology transfers to Ukraine.

The 101st Missile Brigade , which is equipped with the Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile system, was recently deployed to Belarus. The Kremlin threatened Germany with direct strikes on its military production facilities in Berlin, following German accusations that Moscow orchestrated an attempted explosive drone attack at Leipzig Airport last month.

The Russians have threatened British drone manufacturing facilities with a “semi-military response” over the transfer of missile blueprints to Ukraine. They also threaten to take unspecified “additional measures” in response to Norway’s expanding military presence along its northern border with Russia.

Although Putin may have convinced Trump that he has “ no hostile plans ” towards Europe, his actions suggest otherwise.

Option three — the most dangerous — would be to continue his failed summer offensive into the fall. He can then weaponize winter once again by attacking Ukraine’s critical infrastructure in an effort to put Ukrainian civilians in the cold.

Why is it the most dangerous? One reason is that the Kremlin is struggling to replace its battlefield losses and may be forced to mobilize as many as 600,000 soldiers after the State Duma elections later this month. They are waiting until after the election for a reason — the public may not take it well.

Putin’s generals are also 0 for 15 when it comes to securing the Donbas. The Kyiv Independent reports those same generals are trying to postpone their deadline from New Year’s Day to March 31, 2027. The Institute for the Study of War pushes the likelihood of that happening out to 2032, given “their current rate of advance — if they can seize it at all.”

Russian doctrine calls for mass in soldiers and artillery. More meat assaults are on the horizon. With Russian casualties now exceeding 1.5 million , 2 million casualties this time next year is a grim likelihood.

Putin’s last option — and the least likely — is to simply declare victory, stop bombing Ukraine and withdraw Russian forces back to their February 2022 border.

Team Trump needs to understand that when Putin says he wants peace, he means he wants the complete annihilation of Ukraine — the country, the language, the culture, and the resistance to his hegemony.

His terms remained the same after his meeting with Witkoff and Kushner — just repackaged. His demand for three days of cease-fire afforded Putin the opportunity to stockpile his ballistic missile inventory and strike Kyiv when the Washington suits departed.

Putin believes he is winning. That is what his generals are telling him — not because he is winning, but because providing him an accurate description of the battlefield would be hazardous to their health.

On Sunday, he repeated to reporters what his generals told him: Russian troops had captured Sviatohirsk in Ukraine’s Donetsk region. On Monday, the commander of Ukraine’s Third Army Corps recorded a video in downtown Sviatohirsk, directly refuting their reports.

Trump needs to come to grips with one fact: The only root cause of the war in Ukraine is Putin himself. The only reason this war continues is Putin. He is all-in, and he will escalate to achieve his desired end state, because the alternative is his own demise.

Col. (Ret.) Jonathan Sweet served 30 years as a military intelligence officer and led the U.S. European Command Intelligence Engagement Division from 2012 to 2014. Mark Toth writes on national security and foreign policy. They are the cofounders of INTREP360 and the INTREP360 Intelligence Report on Substack.

articles.title: Trump, Fetterman deliver surprises at RNC night 1
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Trump’s expensive election promise ▪ A rare primary loss for a governor ▪ Apple unveils foldable iPhone ▪ AI researchers issue stark warning President Trump wrapped up the first day of the GOP’s unprecedented midterm convention Wednesday with a lengthy speech reminiscent of his own campaign rallies — delivering on the “Trump-a-palooza” hype. Speakers throughout…
articles.body:
President Trump wrapped up the first day of the GOP’s unprecedented midterm convention Wednesday with a lengthy speech reminiscent of his own campaign rallies — delivering on the “Trump-a-palooza” hype.

Speakers throughout the night praised Trump’s record as he approaches the halfway mark of his second term, while posters of the president adorned the convention center’s walls as baseball caps with his “Make America Great Again” slogan were for sale, The Hill’s Julia Mueller reports from Dallas .

While speaking, Trump reiterated that Republicans should act like he’s on the ballot this November, and those in attendance appeared to be in lockstep with that strategy.

Here’s three big takeaways from the first half of the convention:

Trump promises $5,000 payouts if GOP wins

The biggest piece of news from the president’s keynote speech was his pledge to send $5,000 “Trump dividends” out to all U.S. adults if Republicans hold both the Senate and House in November.

Trump said the money would only be able to be used in the U.S. but didn’t share more specifics. He said he can issue the payments “because we’ve done so well and because our country is making so much money.”

Despite Trump’s promise, the legality and practicality of such a move is unclear. There are about 270 million adults in the U.S., and Congress may have to approve it.

Fox News host Bret Baier estimated in an interview with Vice President Vance following Trump’s speech that the cost would be more than $1.3 trillion to the country, noting some critics may allege this amounts to bribery.

Vance defended the promise by noting the “extraordinary” amount of revenue that has been raised from Trump’s tariffs and that the American people will “share in the benefit.”

Trump has floated similar ideas before, suggesting last year that he would send out $2,000 tariff dividend checks , but it hasn’t come to fruition.

Another moment of the convention that raised eyebrows came when Democratic Sen. John Fetterman (Pa.), who has increasingly been at odds with members of his party, appeared in a video message to introduce his fellow Pennsylvania senator, Dave McCormick (R).

“Why am I here talking to you today?” Fetterman said. “Because, well, I’m a commonsense Democrat.”

He praised McCormick as “the kind of senator who gets the job done.” The two of them have grown increasingly close in recent months and even teamed up earlier this year to launch a joint fundraising committee .

Fetterman said in the video that he would always “reject the extremes in socialism and the anti-American way of life.”

He has been on the outs with many Democrats over bucking the party on key votes and criticizing colleagues to his left. Most recently, he has fallen under scrutiny over a Wall Street Journal report featuring accusations from his former staffers about his alleged lack of commitment to his job responsibilities.

Still, Fetterman confirmed Wednesday that he still plans to caucus with the Democrats in the Senate, as he has said before.

“I’m a lifelong Democrat who votes overwhelmingly with my party—and should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on,” he said.

Cabinet members’ appearances break with norms

In a move that has become commonplace for the Trump administration but is historically rare, several Cabinet members made appearances at the convention, and more are expected today.

That breaks with longstanding norms in which members of the Cabinet generally stay away from overtly political events. Cabinet members are political appointees but are ostensibly prohibited under the Hatch Act from using their offices for political campaign activities.

Among those who appeared on Wednesday were Attorney General Todd Blanche , Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent , Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins and Director of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Mehmet Oz .

The members were notably not introduced by their Cabinet positions as they walked to the podium on stage. For example, Rollins was introduced simply as “the honorable” while Blanche didn’t have any introduction.

Still, the members tore into Democrats as they touted the president and Republicans’ accomplishments.

Blanche focused on the administration’s crackdown on illegal immigration, praising Trump and Vance for their approach. Former Attorney General Eric Holder ripped his successor on Tuesday, calling the planned speech “unprecedented” and “disgraceful.”

“To evil men and women in this country, know this. President Trump will hold you accountable,” Blanche said last night, thanking “Americans for choosing to make our country safe again.”

“They will start by undoing the tremendous achievements of the past two years,” Rollins predicted if Democrats win in November. “The border that has been closed, they will reopen it immediately.”

In 2020, the Office of Special Counsel found multiple Trump officials violated the Hatch Act at that year’s RNC.

▪ The Hill : House GOP leaders take aim at ‘crazy communists’ in speeches.

Today marks the one-year anniversary of the assassination of conservative political activist Charlie Kirk, who was killed while speaking at a Turning Point USA event at Utah Valley University. A memorial is being held today at the university.

Missouri’s redistricting battle returned to the Supreme Court again Wednesday after an appeals court refused to halt a federal judge’s order greenlighting Republicans’ favored congressional map. Here’s an explainer on where the legal battle currently stands .

Steve Feinberg, the low-profile deputy Defense secretary , was interviewed as part of the FBI’s investigation into a CIA officer found with $40 million worth of gold bars at his home, according to NBC News . Feinberg, a private equity titan, had a long professional relationship with David Rush, the intelligence officer accused of running a long con.

Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee speaks at the local Democratic Party headquarters in Johnston, R.I., Nov. 7, 2022. (David Goldman, Associated Press file)

ONE AND DONE: Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee (D) lost his primary election last night to a fellow moderate, former CVS executive Helena Foulkes , whom the governor narrowly defeated in the 2022 primary.

The governor’s downfall is closely linked to his handling of the repairs to the critical Washington Bridge in Providence, which was abruptly closed in 2023, fueling added costs for the state and traffic delays ever since.

The situation made McKee one of the least popular governors in the country: A University of New Hampshire poll from August found his approval rating at only 22 percent among Democrats. The same poll showed Foulkes dominating McKee in a hypothetical primary match-up — 56 percent to the governor’s 18 percent.

McKee is currently on track to lose by about 25 points, as of the latest vote count.

Even though the odds were not good for the Democratic governor ahead of this week’s primary, his defeat is notable as a rare example of a sitting governor losing a reelection bid.

Since 1948, roughly 75 percent of sitting governors won their reelection campaigns, and their success rate has only increased since: from 1948 to 1979, 68 percent of incumbent governors won; from 1980 to 2013, 79 percent won; and from 2014 to 2025, 90 percent won.

Sitting governors who lose their renomination bids are even rarer, with just three examples since 2010: former Nevada Gov. Jim Gibbons (R) in 2010, former Hawaii Gov. Neil Abercrombie (D) in 2014 and former Kansas Gov. Jeff Colyer (R) in 2018.

▪ The Hill : Three takeaways from the primaries.

▪ The Hill : Democratic socialist ousts Providence mayor in primary.

BUYBACK REBUFFED : The 10-year yield rose to its highest level in nearly three years, rebuffing Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent ‘s latest effort to push down long-term interest rates.

Bessent announced Wednesday that the Treasury Department would buy back $6 billion of government debt maturing in 10 to 20 years, making good on his promise last month to at least double the standard size of $2 billion per buyback operation.

But some economists said Wall Street likely expected the size of the announcement to be bigger, as much as $7 or $8 billion, which helps explain the market response.

Following the announcement, the 10-year Treasury yield rose 0.05 percentage points — topping 4.85 percent, before settling back around 4.82 percent. The buyback operation will take place this afternoon.

▪ The Hill : 10-year Treasury yields hit multiyear high.

▪ CNBC : Bessent’s political turn tests bond market credibility.

CLOSING OFF : A new proposal from the Trump administration could exclude millions of U.S. residents from the census.

Under the proposed rule posted in the Federal Register on Wednesday, only U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents would be included, leaving out others such as those without lawful status and in the country on a temporary lawful basis, including refugees and people seeking asylum.

The proposal states they should be excluded because they are not “true inhabitants, members of the body politic, or persons with a ‘usual residence’ in the United States due to their lack of a sufficient tie and allegiance to the United States.”

The provision will likely face a legal challenge, as the Constitution’s 14th Amendment states that representatives should be apportioned to the states based on the “whole number of persons” in each state.

The proposal would also drop some questions about race, ethnicity and sexual orientation.

▪ Roll Call : Census overhaul could reshape Congress.

APPLE’S NEW ERA : Apple kicked off a new chapter Wednesday as it unveiled its first foldable iPhone and new CEO John Ternus made his debut appearance.

The long-awaited iPhone Duo will be available on Oct. 23 and retail at $1,999 — the most expensive sticker price yet for an Apple iPhone.

The Duo is a book-style foldable, featuring a bendable display. About the size of a passport, users will be able to view two screens that the company says will be the largest display ever.

Ternus, who had been serving as Apple’s senior vice president of hardware engineering, formally took over for Tim Cook as CEO last week, marking the first leadership change in a decade and a half. Cook has taken a new role as executive chair.

“We brought together thoughtful design with breakthrough engineering in a way only Apple can, and the result is a series of remarkable innovations that we believe will redefine the experience of using a foldable phone,” Ternus said at the launch event.

▪ The Hill : Five takeaways from the event.

HOLIDAY GIFTS : The president gifted White House aide Natalie Harp and two other aides $45,000 cash for Christmastime, according to financial disclosures released by the administration last week.

The payments were made to Harp, who has received significant public scrutiny recently over her close ties to the president, Margo Martin and Chamberlain Harris . All three receive an annual taxpayer-funded salary of $150,000, meaning the gifts equaled almost a third of their salary.

Another White House employee, Oval Office Operations Director Walt Nauta , received a $20,000 gift from Trump.

A federal statute bars federal employees from receiving supplemental income in addition to their salaries, but a White House spokesperson denied these gifts violated any law.

“The gifts at issue here have nothing to do with any of these individuals’ official government duties, and therefore are entirely permissible under relevant legal and ethical standards,” they said.

▪ Forbes : Why some legal experts think the gifts were illegal.

The president will tour the National Medal of Honor Museum in Arlington, Texas, at 1 p.m. EDT and deliver remarks at 1:30 p.m. He will participate in an RNC roundtable in Dallas at 6:15 p.m. and attend the RNC midterm convention at 7 p.m. He will deliver closing remarks at the convention at 9:45 p.m. and then depart Dallas to return to the White House.

The Senate will meet at 3 p.m. for a pro forma session.

The House will convene at 3:30 p.m. for a pro forma session.

Pages from the Anthropic website and the company’s logo are displayed on a computer screen in New York, Feb. 26, 2026. (Patrick Sison, Associated Press)

EXISTENTIAL THREAT : Multiple current and former researchers for the AI company Anthropic have raised eyebrows this week with warnings that the technology has the potential to destroy humanity in the future.

Jacob Coxon , a former researcher for Anthropic and OpenAI, initiated the string of comments Tuesday with a thread on the social platform X in which he accused the companies of “gambling with our lives.” He said he resigned from Anthropic on the same day he made the post.

“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he said.

Coxon said many at OpenAI haven’t “deeply internalized the civilizational stakes,” while Anthropic leaders understand the stakes but believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must move forward despite the risks.

Several current Anthropic researchers quickly echoed Coxon’s warnings.

Evan Hubinger , who leads alignment science for Anthropic, said on X that “we really do believe AI could kill all humans.” He said he personally believes the chance is greater than 10 percent in the next decade.

He said Anthropic is trying its best, but the company doesn’t yet have a plan to ensure superintelligence stays aligned with human interests.

Samuel Marks , the head of scalable oversight for the company, said AI developers believe their technology could cause “human extinction” in the next few years.

“I work on safety research at Anthropic because I hope my work will reduce the chance of these extinction-level bad outcomes,” he said.

The comments are the latest warnings about the potential dangers that AI could pose, though development has continued full steam ahead. More than 1,300 employees at top AI companies signed onto an open lawyer in July calling on the federal government to support an international effort to pace automated AI development.

Anthropic and OpenAI both supported that effort, but are still racing against each other and other companies to develop AI technology and secure more funding.

A motorboat passes a general cargo ship anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Sept. 6, 2026. (Vahid Salemi, Associated Press)

READY TO FIGHT BACK : Iran appears poised to fight back against growing U.S. leverage in the Strait of Hormuz, sending gas prices to their highest levels in months amid renewed concerns of escalating fighting, The Hill’s Ellen Mitchell and Laura Kelly report .

Oil prices rose to more than $100 a barrel Wednesday for the first time since July, with national gas prices averaging just above $4.22, up from $4.15 a gallon on Tuesday and $4.12 a gallon a week ago.

The Trump administration has worked to open passageways through the strait to usher oil out, and more ships have been making it through the vital passageway. But as the U.S. targeted Iranian vessels trying to export oil, American assets and allies in the region came under renewed attack, escalating fears of a renewed conflict.

Experts tell Mitchell and Kelly that the fighting is only likely to increase in the near term and the U.S. cracks down.

“Ironically, the harder the U.S. pushes to get the strait back open, the harder Iran pushes back, leading to heightened escalation, fewer ships passing, and higher oil prices as a result,” said Mona Yacoubian , director and senior adviser of the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank.

Trump brushed off questions Wednesday about the high oil prices, telling reporters he thinks Iran is holding out until after the midterm election to come to the table.

“Yes, a negotiation could possibly happen, but it’s not something we’re looking at. This war will immediately end after our election,” Trump said, adding that he expects oil prices “to be tumbling downward” after the midterms.

He also warned more attacks on Iran were coming: “You’re going to see a lot more.”

articles.title: The man who forced Congress to care for 9/11 survivors
articles.summary: Twenty-five years after the attacks, twice as many people have died from illnesses linked to World Trade Center exposure as were killed on September 11 itself.
articles.body:
On September 17, 2001, construction supervisor John Feal was working atop “the pile,” helping clear the wreckage of the World Trade Center. As he guided trucks backing up to haul away twisted steel, an 8,000-pound beam suddenly broke loose, crashing onto Feal’s foot.

“Blood sprayed in every direction,” he recalls.

When fellow rescue workers pulled off his boot, bones were protruding through his sock. “I’ll be back in a couple of hours,” Feal reassured everyone before being taken away by ambulance.

He never returned to Ground Zero. Instead, he began a different battle — one that would ultimately shape the lives of tens of thousands of people exposed to the toxic aftermath of 9/11.

Feal spent months in hospitals, enduring surgery after surgery to save his leg, ultimately losing half his foot. Because he had been volunteering at Ground Zero, his medical bills weren’t covered. He applied to the first iteration of the federally funded Victim Compensation Fund, but he was denied. Feal was forced to sell nearly everything he owned.

He began attending group therapy for 9/11 responders, but instead of trauma, they talked about liquidating retirement accounts and their children’s college tuition funds to pay medical debt.

And they were getting sick, with respiratory diseases, digestive disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder and aggressive cancers. Many had been healthy before spending months digging through the rubble, with no family history of the diseases that were suddenly disabling or killing them.

The collapse of the Twin Towers released a massive toxic dust cloud . Hundreds of hazardous substances blanketed Lower Manhattan, with microscopic particles penetrating even protective gear.

Few Americans understood the danger. Public officials, including EPA Administrator Christine Todd Whitman , repeatedly assured New Yorkers that the air was “safe.” Scientists later compared the dust’s alkalinity to Drano and linked World Trade Center exposure to an expanding list of chronic illnesses.

Feal began to understand that he was witnessing a community-wide crisis. “Someone had to fight for them,” he thought. That someone would be him.

Feal threw a boot on his damaged foot and headed to Washington, believing lawmakers would be supportive. Instead, he encountered dismissal and denial. He kept hearing a familiar refrain: “John, thank you for your service. Now, if you’ll excuse me, I’m running late for a meeting. God bless.”

Then, in 2006 at just 34 years old, NYPD Detective James Zadroga died. Zadroga had spent more than 450 hours working on the debris pile before developing a devastating respiratory disease. Forensic testing later found asbestos, lead, benzene, and glass fibers in his lungs.

Armed with that evidence, Feal returned to Washington with teams of responders. They fanned across Capitol Hill, sometimes packing more than 50 meetings into a single day. Some arrived with oxygen tanks or in wheelchairs. Others died within weeks of testifying before Congress.

The objections became familiar. Lawmakers questioned the science; Feal brought the studies . They warned of fraud ; he demanded proof. Wasn’t this New York’s responsibility? Feal countered that responders had come from a ll over the country.

And it wasn’t just responders who were suffering. As many as 400,000 residents, office workers and students had been exposed, and had since dispersed across every state and Puerto Rico.

In December 2010, Congress passed the James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Act , creating the first federally funded World Trade Center Health Program and reopened the Victim Compensation Fund , which had closed in 2003.

It was a landmark victory, but an incomplete one. The law excluded many cancers, covered too narrow a geographic area and imposed a five-year deadline on illnesses that could take decades to emerge.

On June 11, 2019, Feal returned to Capitol Hill, believing there was one final chance.

The subcommittee hearing room overflowed as television cameras lined the walls. Witness after witness described terminal cancer, financial ruin, and loved ones already lost. Yet many members of Congress never came to the hearing. Their empty chairs became almost as powerful as the testimonies themselves.

Then the final witness, talk show host Jon Stewart , who had used his platform to amplify the fight, took his seat.

“Behind me: a room filled with 9/11 first responders,” he gestured. “And in front of me: A nearly empty Congress. Sick and dying, they brought themselves down here to speak — to no one.”

Stewart closed the emotional nine-minute speech with a direct challenge to Congress. “They did their jobs with courage, grace, tenacity, humility. Eighteen years later — do yours!”

His blistering condemnation of congressional indifference proved decisive. Within weeks, Congress overwhelmingly passed the Never Forget the Heroes Act , which President Trump signed it into law.

Today, Feal and advocates still fight to protect the funds from what they see as renewed threats from the Trump administration. Feal’s new memoir, “ I Will Follow You Anywhere ,” chronicles these concerns, but its larger story is the extraordinary grassroots campaign that made the funds possible in the first place.

Twenty-five years after the attacks, twice as many people have died from illnesses linked to World Trade Center exposure as were killed on September 11 itself. Thousands receive care through the funds, while researchers continue to document new illnesses associated with exposure to the toxic dust.

America promised never to forget the people who died on September 11. Feal spent the next quarter century making sure it did not forget the people who survived.

Ray Stanton is a freelance writer and award-winning author.

articles.title: House panel to probe foreign ‘Trojan horses’ as Singham scrutiny widens
articles.summary: House lawmakers will examine alleged foreign malign influence operations, including campaigns tied to China, Cuba and U.S. data centers.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Congressional scrutiny of foreign influence operations in the United States is widening, with a powerful panel of lawmakers set to hold a hearing next week examining how nonprofits and activist networks serve as potential "Trojan horses" for foreign adversaries. Fox News Digital has learned the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on South and Central Asia has scheduled an open hearing for Tuesday titled "Trojan Horses: Covert Foreign Malign Influence Operations in America." "This is a critically important topic right now because the vectors for foreign influence in our public discourse are greater than they've ever been before, in large part because of social media," Sam Lyman, head of research at the Bitcoin Policy Institute and one of the hearing's planned witnesses, told Fox News Digital. "Social media acts as a gain-of-function for mind viruses that are incubated overseas and oftentimes find their way over to the United States," said Lyman, a former senior advisor and speechwriter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. The planned hearing, which takes its name from the mythological horse Greek soldiers hid inside of to infiltrate the fortified city of Troy, is expected to include a scrutiny of influence from China and Cuba to the Islamic Republic of Iran and pro-Palestinian groups. It marks an expansion of congressional scrutiny of foreign influence beyond the tax and financial questions already being pursued by the House Ways and Means Committee, which has subpoenaed three nonprofits in a network funded by Neville Roy Singham, an American-born communist tech tycoon now based in Shanghai. Mike Gonzalez, a senior fellow at the Heritage Foundation who is scheduled to testify as a witness, told Fox News Digital the threat is real. "Adversaries and outright enemies of the United States such as China and Cuba, shadowy non-government organizations surreptitiously implanting Islamism – and even friendlier countries such as Mexico, which tries to use its diaspora populations for lobbying – take advantage of the open nature of our society to infiltrate and influence America." Evidence of foreign influence abounds throughout society, he said. "They do it in the K-12 educational system that instructs our entire population, the institutions of higher education that produce our leaders, the government agencies that make up our government, the lobbying firms that write far too many of our laws, the museums that exist to transmit our heritage to future generations, etc.," Gonzalez said. The Senate Judiciary Committee, House Oversight Committee and the House Select Committee on China have also investigated the issue of malign foreign influence. Singham hasn't responded to repeated requests for comment. The Foreign Affairs Subcommittee, which oversees the State Department's Office of Public Diplomacy, now promises to ask the larger national-security question behind those financial investigations: whether America's open political system and nonprofit sector are being exploited as Trojan horses by foreign governments seeking to influence American politics, public opinion and strategic policy from within. Earlier this year, the Office of Public Diplomacy, led by Undersecretary Sarah Rodgers, issued the subcommittee a report about foreign "vectors" of influence in the U.S. In March, Fox News Digital published a five-part investigation that mapped 223 transactions totaling $591 million across five continents from 2017 through 2025 through 67 core organizations in the Singham network that act like an inner hub for a constellation of an estimated 2,000 groups worldwide, pushing pro-China, anti-American propaganda, including the communist Party for Socialism and Liberation. The investigation documented how Singham directly poured $285 million into an activist network of six pro-China, pro-communist nonprofit organizations, starting in 2017 – Breakthrough BT Media Inc., CodePink Women for Peace, Justice and Education Fund Inc., People's Forum Inc., People's Support Foundation Ltd. and Tricontinenental Ltd. As Fox News Digital first reported in June, the Justice Department is investigating alleged financial crimes connected to Singham and the nonprofit organizations he funded, with the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York opening a grand jury investigation into Singham's money. Singham and the nonprofits have denied taking direction from the Chinese government, and neither Singham nor the organizations have been charged with crimes. Rep. Bill Huizenga, R-Mich., chairs the South and Central Asia subcommittee, while Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove, D-Calif., serves as ranking member. Republican members include Reps. James Moylan of Guam, Jefferson Shreve of Indiana, Thomas Kean Jr. of New Jersey, Scott Perry of Pennsylvania, Tim Burchett of Tennessee, Keith Self of Texas and Michael Baumgartner of Washington. Democratic members include Reps. Ami Bera of California, Kweisi Mfume of Maryland, Pramila Jayapal of Washington, George Latimer of New York and Julie Johnson of Texas. HOUSE COMMITTEE PASSES FOREIGN FUNDING TRANSPARENCY ACT TO EXPOSE FOREIGN DONATIONS TO NONPROFITS The hearing puts the investigation under the umbrella of House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., whose committee has made confronting the Chinese Communist Party and strengthening U.S. defenses against Beijing a central focus. Earlier this year, Mast joined lawmakers from both parties in pressing the Trump administration to tighten export controls aimed at restricting China's access to advanced semiconductor manufacturing technology. The three scheduled witnesses invited by Republican lawmakers to testify at the hearing bring together three different fronts in the emerging foreign-influence investigation: Cuba's influence infrastructure inside the United States, the Chinese Communist Party's broader political and technological strategy and campaigns by the Singham network targeting America's artificial-intelligence and data-center buildout. DOJ, TREASURY INVESTIGATE NONPROFITS AND LEADERS ALLEGEDLY COORDINATING WITH CUBA IN INFLUENCE CAMPAIGN Gonzalez is expected to speak on Cuba's alleged influence network in the United States. "Cuba is 100% operating a foreign influence operation in the U.S.," Gonzalez told Fox News Digital earlier this year, describing the communist island as "ground zero for anti-American revolutionary organizing in the Western Hemisphere." Gonzalez said investigators should determine whether American organizations crossed the line between constitutionally protected activism and political activity coordinated by a foreign government. INSIDE CUBA’S FOREIGN INFLUENCE CAMPAIGN: FROM THE '60S VENCEREMOS BRIGADE TO A CALIFORNIA UNION HALL A Fox News Digital investigation identified an ecosystem of U.S. organizations supporting Cuba that overlaps significantly with the Singham network. CodePink, the People's Forum, BreakThrough News, Tricontinental, the ANSWER Coalition and the Party for Socialism and Liberation have all been key players supporting the Communist Party of Cuba and developed close relationships with Cuba and its state institutions. Gonzalez has written specifically about that intersection. A second witness, Jamestown Foundation senior fellow Matthew Johnson, brings expertise on the Chinese Communist Party. Johnson specializes in China's elite politics, strategic thinking, technology policy and the party-state's control over China's financial sector and private economy. His research has examined the relationship between CCP ideology, propaganda, political control and China's technology strategy. FIRST ON FOX: ‘NO KINGS’ PROTEST NETWORK BEHIND FIGHT AGAINST AI DATA CENTERS AND FLOCK CAMERAS The third witness, Lyman, has investigated another front of the same battle: the campaign against America's AI and data-center infrastructure. Lyman co-authored research identifying the Singham network, and particularly the Party for Socialism and Liberation, as a significant force in protests against data centers around the country. His research identified 21 campaigns across 14 states and calculated that about $23.6 billion in proposed AI and data-center investment had been delayed, reduced or blocked in campaigns in which the Party for Socialism and Liberation was a significant mobilizing force. The research described a broader information environment in which Chinese state media criticized the environmental and economic effects of American data centers while Beijing subsidized the expansion of its own AI infrastructure. Lyman has argued that legitimate debate over AI safety, energy use and data-center construction should be insulated from influence by geopolitical competitors seeking an advantage over the United States. House Ways and Means Chairman Jason Smith, R-Mo., has described the organizations as part of a "foreign-aligned influence network" and is investigating whether some tax-exempt groups are functioning as agents of foreign interests. His committee recently issued subpoenas to the People's Forum, Tricontinental and BreakThrough BT Media after months of seeking records about their funding, foreign contacts and relationships with Singham. The organizations refused to produce documents in response to the subpoenas, saying they were the targets of a "witch hunt." articles.title: Missouri Secretary of State faces contempt hearing amid redistricting fight
articles.summary: Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins (R) is set to appear before the state Supreme Court on Thursday as judges weigh whether to hold him in contempt amid an escalating battle over the state’s congressional map. Late Wednesday night, a federal judge rejected the state’s request to stop the morning proceedings. “Numerous considerations counsel this Court against…
articles.body:
Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins (R) is set to appear before the state Supreme Court on Thursday as judges weigh whether to hold him in contempt amid an escalating battle over the state’s congressional map .

Late Wednesday night, a federal judge rejected the state’s request to stop the morning proceedings.

“Numerous considerations counsel this Court against enjoining a state court of last resort, particularly before it even conducts a hearing,” U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark wrote in a brief order.

“For starters, the Supreme Court of Missouri is a fellow court, and a court of a separate sovereign. And enjoining another court’s hearing is an extraordinary measure that pretermits that court’s decision—that court could deny the relief requested, or hold any ruling in abeyance pending further federal proceedings,” he added.

Missouri officials took the unusual step earlier Wednesday of asking Clark to intervene and “bar the Missouri Supreme Court’s attempt to punish Secretary Hoskins for complying with this Court’s order.”

Republican Attorney General Catherine Hanaway’s office argued that the judge had authority to block the proceedings under an exception in the Anti-Injunction Act that allows federal courts to step in when necessary to “protect or effectuate” its judgements.

“Despite von Glahn’s antics, this case is not particularly complicated,” her office wrote.

“This Court — a federal court — has given Secretary Hoskins an order — under federal law — to implement the HB 1 map for the 2026 General Election. That governs over a state court order —relying only on state law — to use a different congressional map for the 2026 General Election,” the motion continued.

Richard von Glahn, who launched the initial challenge against the GOP-favored lines, asked the Missouri Supreme Court on Tuesday to hold Hoskins in contempt for violating a Sept. 3 order that barred the use of the new map for the November contests.

His attorneys asserted that Clark lacked jurisdiction to stop the Missouri Supreme Court’s hearing, which it cast as “fundamentally different” in scope.

“The Missouri Supreme Court ’s contempt proceeding does not relitigate anything the federal court decided,” they wrote. “The state court is not asking whether the Secretary has a right to use the HB 1 map — it is asking whether the Secretary is in contempt of the state’s highest court.”

That map would’ve created a 7-1 GOP advantage, handing the party a potential pickup opportunity in the midterms.

Republicans appealed the Missouri court’s decision to the U.S. Supreme Court , but Justice Brett Kavanaugh declined on Tuesday to intervene. His one-line order offered no explanation.

A few hours later, Clark issued a temporary restraining order in a separate lawsuit brought by Rep. Rob Onder (R-Mo.) that prohibited state election officials from using anything other than the newly drawn boundaries, saying it was necessary to avoid widespread voter confusion.

Hoskins cited that decision in a Tuesday evening email to local election officials, instructing them to move forward under the GOP-favored map. He wrote that the federal ruling “takes precedence” over the Missouri Supreme Court’s order.

Von Glahn argued that it didn’t and asked the state Supreme Court to force Hoskins to comply with its order.

“This Court should make clear that regardless of other orders (except from the United States Supreme Court) the Missouri Secretary of State must comply with this court’s injunction,” von Glahn’s attorney wrote in court filings. “The Court should instruct all local election authorities that HB 1 is not the law and has never been the law.”

Missouri Chief Justice W. Brent Howell has ordered Hoskins to appear in person on Thursday morning to explain why he should not be held in contempt.

Shortly after, Hoskins wrote on social platform X that he “look[ed] forward to my day in court.”

“Missouri is and always will be the place I call home,” the Republican wrote. “I will always fight to protect our common-sense Missouri values from a liberal Democrat Socialist and his out-of-state NYC sugar daddies.”

He added, “I will continue to abide by Judge Clark’s federal temporary restraining order on a federal congressional election.”

articles.title: Too easy to fake: US needs stricter screening for marriage visas
articles.summary: The Department of Justice has unsealed an indictment describing a large-scale marriage fraud network that has operated for more than a decade, conspiring “to orchestrate more than 1,000 sham marriages to fraudulently obtain immigration status for foreign nationals.”
articles.body:
This August, the Department of Justice unsealed an indictment describing a large-scale marriage fraud network that has operated for more than a decade.

The indictment charges 11 individuals with conspiring “to orchestrate more than 1,000 sham marriages to fraudulently obtain immigration status for foreign nationals, primarily citizens of the People’s Republic of China.” Clients allegedly paid up to $100,000 for services; the organization is believed to have collected tens of millions of dollars from these illegal activities.

Services allegedly include finding a willing U.S. citizen for the marriage. Citizens are used because the spouse of a citizen gets immediate relative status, and immigrant visas for immediate relatives are unlimited. The network coached clients on how to conceal the true nature of their relationship if they were interviewed, and manufactured wedding photographs, joint bank accounts and apartment leases to provide evidence that the spouses had bona fide marriages.

This is why convincing paperwork alone does not necessarily establish that a marriage is genuine.

A citizen filing a Form I-130, Petition for Alien Relative for a spouse “ must show by a preponderance of the evidence that the marriage was legally valid and bona fide at its inception and not entered for the purpose of evading the immigration laws.”

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services may interview the spouses and request additional evidence to determine whether their relationship is genuine. If fraud is suspected, the petition may be referred to the agency’s Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate. The directorate may visit homes and workplaces and take other steps to determine whether the marriage is a sham, as well as obtain subpoenas for documents.

Congress enacted the Immigration Marriage Fraud Amendments of 1986 to deter such fraudulent unions. Among other things, it amended the Immigration and Nationality Act to make a grant of permanent resident status conditional if the marriage it is based on was entered into fewer than 24 months before resident status was granted.

The amendments also subject alien spouses to the risk of being put in removal proceedings if it is determined that their marriage is a sham, and prohibit the approval of future visa petitions for an alien who “has previously been accorded, or has sought to be accorded,” resident status on the basis of a marriage determined to have been “entered into for the purpose of evading the immigration law.”

In September 2022, the U.S. Government Accountability Office released a report that made recommendations for improving the anti-fraud program, including with respect to marriage fraud. According to the office’s recommendation tracker , which was updated in February 2026, four of the six recommendations were still open, meaning they had not been fully implemented. The four open recommendations advise U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to evaluate fraud risks regularly; evaluate and update anti-fraud activities regularly; develop a process for evaluating its anti-fraud strategy; and establish outcome-oriented performance measures.

In addition to civil immigration consequences, the sentences for a criminal marriage fraud are imprisonment for up to five years and a fine of up to $250,000, or both. The agency should increase the deterrent value of these sanctions by working with the Justice Department to publicize the sentences and fines actually imposed.

The agency has frequently waived in-person interviews in recent years, but it updated its policy manual last year on when an interview is needed, such as when evidence is missing, material inconsistencies are found, or there are other significant indications that the marriage is a sham.

Interviews can be very effective in determining marriage fraud, but they are more difficult when spouses have been coached on how they should answer questions. If initial processing raises suspicion that the marriage might be a sham, a Stokes interview should be conducted. A Stokes interview is more likely to identify a sham marriage than routine interviews because it puts the spouses in separate rooms, asks them the same 50 to 100 questions about things a married couple should know, and then compares their answers.

Before denying a petition on account of material discrepancies, the couple should be given a chance to explain material discrepancies and to offer additional evidence.

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services should complete the implementation of the Government Accountability Office’s recommendation as soon as possible, conduct Stokes interviews for cases with specific fraud indicators, and publicize the consequences of using a sham marriage to obtain lawful resident status.

Nolan Rappaport was detailed to the House Judiciary Committee as an executive branch immigration law expert for three years. He subsequently served as an immigration counsel for the Subcommittee on Immigration, Border Security and Claims for four years. Prior to working on the Judiciary Committee, he wrote decisions for the Board of Immigration Appeals for 20 years.

articles.title: On the Ballot: One year after Charlie Kirk’s assassination, Turning Point USA presses on
articles.summary: Turning Point USA (TPUSA) is navigating its first election cycle without its founder. Thursday marks one year since Charlie Kirk was assassinated at a Utah university during one of his “Prove Me Wrong” debates. His wife, Erika Kirk, took the reins of conservative nonprofit after his death, charting its course as the leading youth organization in Republican politics. …
articles.body:
Turning Point USA (TPUSA) is navigating its first election cycle without its founder.

Thursday marks one year since Charlie Kirk was assassinated at a Utah university during one of his “Prove Me Wrong” debates. His wife, Erika Kirk , took the reins of conservative nonprofit after his death, charting its course as the leading youth organization in Republican politics.

TPUSA says it has only grown since Kirk’s death, yet Republicans acknowledge Charlie Kirk’s death has left a void few in the party can fill.

“He wanted people who felt lost to know the everlasting hope he found through faith and the sense of meaning and purpose that can fill the deeper longings we so often try to satisfy elsewhere,” Erika Kirk wrote in an op-ed for The New York Times published on Monday.

“To the world, he was Charlie Kirk,” she wrote. “But to me, he was the love of my life. To our children, he was the center of their world.”

Turning Point USA is convening in Orem, Utah at Utah Valley University on Thursday to commemorate the one-year anniversary of Charlie Kirk’s death, after a gunman fatally shot the conservative activist at the school during his “The American Comeback Tour.”

Thursday’s event, called “Freedom Built to Last,” will include guest appearances from figures like conservative commentator Glenn Beck, Christian apologist and Charlie Kirk mentor Frank Turek, among others.

Republicans are also planning to honor Charlie Kirk on Thursday evening, during the second day of their midterm convention in Dallas, which looks to touch on the TPUSA founder’s “impact on American youth and converting that legacy into a call to mobilize voters.”

Started in 2012, TPUSA is regarded as one of the most dominant youth-focused conservative organizations in the country, with its founder making a name for himself as he traveled to college campuses to debate students and push back against liberal talking points.

But the political nonprofit morphed into a serious power player in recent election cycles as a part of Republicans’ voter outreach infrastructure, so much so that President Trump and Vice President Vance have credited Kirk and his organization for their electoral victories.

“I want to express my tremendous gratitude to Charlie Kirk,” Trump said at a TPUSA event in December 2024, describing Kirk as “an amazing guy.”

“And his whole staff for their relentless efforts to achieve this very historic victory. It’s such a great honor,” he added. “It’s not my victory. It’s your victory.”

Guest-hosting a special episode of “The Charlie Kirk Show” just days after the conservative activist was murdered, Vance remarked that “if it weren’t for Charlie Kirk, I would not be the Vice President of the United States.”

The Hill reached out to several TPUSA officials for comment.

The conservative nonprofit has grown over the last year. TPUSA saw a 64 percent increase within the last year in the number of college chapters operating across the country, CNN reported , citing an internal document it obtained. The news outlet noted that the organization has seen three times as many high school clubs.

The influential youth-based political group is also still raking in cash, with the nonprofit seeing a 30-percent revenue increase during fiscal 2025 compared to the year prior, according to the Arizona Republic . Turning Point PAC, meanwhile, has also outraised itself by several million dollars in recent years, the Arizona news outlet noted.

And TPUSA has made it clear that the organization will be a key player in the 2028 Republican presidential primary. Erika Kirk preemptively endorsed Vance in December for the Republican contest, even though the vice president has not formally declared a bid.

Vance has sidestepped questions around a possible White House bid, emphasizing he’s focused on the midterms. Yet there’s early indicators of a political infrastructure forming behind the scenes.

“We are going to get my husband’s friend, JD Vance, elected for 48 in the most resounding way possible,” Erika Kirk said during Turning Point USA’s AmericaFest conference in Phoenix.

articles.title: Charlie Kirk statue bound for NY's Times Square as sculptor defies threats ahead of unveiling
articles.summary: Sergio Furnari's $100,000 bronze Charlie Kirk memorial will be unveiled in Times Square on the one-year anniversary of the assassination Thursday afternoon.
articles.body: An Italian-born sculpture artist is set to unveil a six-figure tribute to Charlie Kirk in the heart of New York City this week — a move that he hopes will spark dialogue rather than division. Sergio Furnari was still in bed when his daughter came home with the news that Kirk had been assassinated at a Turning Point USA event at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025. "It took me a couple of seconds to connect," Furnari told Fox News Digital. "And then I kind of was, I would say, saddened by it." ERIKA KIRK REFLECTS ON FIRST YEAR OF GRIEF AFTER CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION IN NYT ESSAY Within weeks, Furnari — who gained attention for his 40-foot sculpture of athlete Cristiano Ronaldo — was fielding calls suggesting he create a tribute to Kirk. "I was like, ‘No way, I cannot get involved with politics,’" Furnari said. "But I [saw] how Erika [Kirk] got treated, including the parents of Charlie, and that’s what I think became my catalyzer[sic]." ERIKA KIRK COMFORTS A STRANGER IN TEARS DURING HEARING FOR HUSBAND'S ACCUSED ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON "If you’re a parent, no matter if you were Democrat or Republican, you should have a little bit of empathy," he continued. Furnari got to work on the memorial — a 6-foot,-5-inch sculpture painted bronze and funded by his own savings. "I did the first one in early December," Furnari said. "It came out good, different than [the final] one, and without a microphone. For me, it was just to test my skills." "From there on, I became more passionate about it — just because of the way everybody was making fun of him," he added. "I feel like they killed him once, and they kill him each time, over and over again." A YEAR AFTER CHARLIE KIRK'S MURDER, SOME COMICS ARE CALLING OUT JOKES ABOUT HIS DEATH Within five months, the statue of a seated Kirk holding his famous microphone and wearing a T-shirt with the word "FREEDOM" adorning the front was complete. However, the tribute also came with a monumental cost of $100,000, which was paid for by Furnari out of his own pocket. INDIANA FARM VOWS TO ‘ABSOLUTELY’ DO CHARLIE KIRK CORN MAZE AGAIN DESPITE WAVE OF BACKLASH "If I include my time, [it was] probably more than $100,000," Furnari told Fox News Digital, adding, "It sounds like a number that is like, ‘Oh my God,’ because there are people that don’t know the value of art." Furnari is still looking to recoup the cost of the project and has launched an online fundraiser to crowdfund support, with the promise that "donors of any kind will have their name engraved on the monument’s platform." HE FLED COMMUNISM. NOW THIS CALIFORNIA MAYOR IS HONORING CHARLIE KIRK AND REFUSING TO BACK DOWN Despite the eye-watering price tag, Furnari insists that he is not an avid supporter of Kirk. "It’s not like I agree with him. There’s a lot of stuff I didn’t agree with," Furnari said. "But still, freedom of expression and, in my case, freedom of creation — there are no boundaries, no borders. That’s where we kind of stand together." The statue of Kirk is set to be unveiled in New York City’s Times Square on Sept. 10 at 2:33 p.m. to mark the one-year anniversary — down to the minute — of the conservative activist’s assassination. "There’s lots of New Yorkers, millions of New Yorkers, who love Charlie," Furnari told Fox News Digital. "So come on by." 'ARE YOU EFFING KIDDING ME?' CALIFORNIA RESIDENTS REACT TO STREET BEING RENAMED AFTER CHARLIE KIRK The artist also revealed he has received countless hate-filled messages in response to the memorial, with some individuals even threatening to deface the statue at the unveiling and mocking the way in which Kirk was assassinated. "I get thousands, probably hundreds of thousands of comments, like, ‘Where is the hole?’ or ‘I will make sure you will find his head in your bed,’" Furnari said, adding, "Nobody really scares me. And when they threaten my life, it’s like whatever." Furnari insists that the message behind the statue is apolitical, and his hope is that the tribute to Kirk will inspire both tolerance and creativity in the wake of his death. articles.title: Presidential flip? GOP insider predicts Trump change of mind on key AI policy ahead of midterms
articles.summary: Trump ally Amy Kremer predicts President Donald Trump will shift on AI data centers after hearing from Americans on the midterm campaign trail.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: A GOP insider making the conservative case for regulating artificial intelligence development predicts President Donald Trump’s full-throated support for data center expansion will soon change after he hears from the American people on the midterm campaign trail. In an interview with Fox News Digital, Amy Kremer, a close Trump ally, Republican National Committee member and founder of "Humans First," warned that the voice of the average American is being left out of the ongoing AI data center debate. She believes that is about to change as the president prepares to hit the campaign trail in support of Republicans ahead of the midterms this fall. Right now, Kremer asserted that Trump is "only hearing one side of the story from big tech." "He's getting ready to go out on the campaign trail, and I think he's going to hear more from the American people on the data center side of things. And I hope he does," she said, adding, "I know the president, and his heart, and he would not like the way the Americans are being treated." MAGA BEGINS TO CRACK AS 2026 GOP ROSTER BACKS AWAY FROM TRUMP'S TECH VISION Kremer was pivotal in founding the modern Tea Party movement and through the years established several pro-Trump political action committees, including the "Great America PAC," the first and largest grassroots organization founded in 2016 to support then-candidate Trump. Now, she is the chairwoman of "Humans First," a political group calling for an "America First approach to AI" that it says would keep the U.S. ahead of China while protecting American families, communities and jobs. She said that while Trump has made it clear that he wants America to lead on AI development, she believes that innovation and safety are "not mutually exclusive." "I love the president. He has been an amazing president. I know he wants us to lead the world in technology and innovation, and I support him in that," she said, while noting, "There's this narrative out there that [with] innovation, you have to forego safety, and it's just not accurate. It's not true." TEA PARTY FOUNDER LAUNCHES NATIONWIDE 'DATA CENTER REVOLT' AGAINST AI DATA CENTER EXPANSION As the GOP gathers in Dallas for its first midterm convention, Humans First unveiled a new data center policy outline that it is urging the president and Republicans in Congress and state legislatures to adopt. The plan, obtained exclusively by Fox News Digital, calls for greater local control over data center development and rejects the use of eminent domain for land seizures. The plan opposes federal and state "efforts to strip communities of that authority," including through a federal data center moratorium, which many opponents of AI development have called for. Instead, the plan calls for local communities to be given the ability to welcome or reject new data center developments through zoning and land-use processes. Additionally, the plan rejects what it describes as "blank-check tax breaks" and subsidies and states that "any incentives must be transparent and tied to enforceable benefits for the community." The plan calls for full transparency on data center development, stating that "before approval, communities deserve to know the project's end user, electricity demand, water use, land requirements, infrastructure costs, tax incentives, permanent jobs and environmental impacts." It also calls for protection for ratepayers so that families and small businesses do not pay higher electric bills. Instead, it states that data centers should pay the full cost of the power generation, transmission, grid upgrades and infrastructure they require. TRUMP SAYS GOVERNORS, MAYORS SHOULD WELCOME AI DATA CENTERS NATIONWIDE Two other provisions address some of the most controversial aspects of AI data center development: local water usage and development on farmland, which the plan refers to as a "strategic American resource that should be protected." The way Kremer put it? She posited that "there are more regulations on a hot dog that you buy on a street corner in New York City than there are on these big tech companies with this technology." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "We are not anti-AI, we're not anti-technology, and we're not anti-data centers," she explained. "What we are is we want the American people to have a seat at the table and a voice in this conversation." articles.title: O’Reilly: ‘Fetterman is going to be a Republican’
articles.summary: Political commentator Bill O’Reilly suggested Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), who once vowed to leave the Democratic Party if its policy position toward Israel changes, “is going to be a Republican.” O’Reilly told NewsNation’s Chris Cuomo late Wednesday that during a previous town hall featuring Fetterman, he recalled telling the senator that he would “have to…
articles.body:
Political commentator Bill O’Reilly suggested Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), who once vowed to leave the Democratic Party if its policy position toward Israel changes, “is going to be a Republican.”

O’Reilly told NewsNation’s Chris Cuomo late Wednesday that during a previous town hall featuring Fetterman, he recalled telling the senator that he would “have to switch parties,” to which the Pennsylvania Democrat did not answer.

“Then I asked him on air too,” he continued. “I said, ‘OK, when are you switching parties?’ He will. He’s going to be a Republican.”

The former Fox News host also noted that Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.) asked his colleague to speak in a video shown at the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) midterm convention in Dallas.

O’Reilly went on to say that President Trump’s tariffs on steel “has injected a lot of money and hope into” Pennsylvania’s steel industry.

“So, McCormick asked Fetterman, ‘Hey, we owe it to the folks for you to get out there and say that, which Fetterman did,” he told Cuomo and sports commentator Stephen A. Smith.

The commentator added later that it would be ironic “if the Democrats take the House by two and then Fetterman flips to the Republican Party, which means the tie and [Vice President] JD Vance is the tiebreaker.” Unsure of this, the NewsNation host replied that he was “taking all action on that wager.”

Fetterman has grown to be one of the Democrat Party’s most outspoken centrist critics , lambasting left-wing candidates for their progressive views and differences with him over the state of Israel. He frequently appears on conservative media to criticize and provide commentary about changes within the caucus.

The Pennsylvania Democrat, in the clip shown at the convention, branded himself a “commonsense Democrat.”

He praised McCormick as “the kind of senator that gets the job done,” noting their work with Trump to revitalize the manufacturing industry in their commonwealth, and that he would always “reject the extremes in socialism and that anti-American way of life.”

His criticisms toward his own party have faced backlash from other Democrats, as Fetterman has been the only Democrat to vote against every Senate war powers resolution seeking to force Trump to wind down the Iran war.

The senator voted in line with Trump 28 percent of the time last year, more than any other Senate Democrat, according to VoteHub .

He said in an interview at The Hill Nation Summit that he would only leave the Democratic Party if it ever became “the anti-Israel party,” himself having become a staunch supporter of the country and its government in the years since the Hamas-led terror attack on Oct. 7, 2023. But Fetterman has also said he would be a “ terrible Republican ” who “votes overwhelmingly with Democrats.”

Constituents have criticized his unyielding support for Israel. A Quinnipiac University survey released in July found that 52 percent of Keystone State voters want Fetterman to leave the Democratic Party.

articles.title: WATCH: Ilhan Omar refuses to address police raid on home her son shares with felon roommate
articles.summary: Ilhan Omar ignored a reporter's questions about a police raid on her son's Minneapolis home that uncovered multiple firearms and ammunition.
articles.body: Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., gave the cold shoulder when asked to weigh in on her son's home being raided by police after his convicted felon roommate was arrested. Minneapolis police officers found, while carrying out a search warrant on August 25, multiple weapons and ammunition in the shared home of Omar's son, Adnan Hirsi, 20, and his roommate Abdulrahman Abdi, 22. The warrant was obtained after Abdi was pulled over in a routine traffic stop and was found to have no driver's license or proof of insurance. Abdi was released, and the car was impounded, but a firearm was later found. As a convicted felon, it is illegal for Abdi to possess a firearm, so the property that he shares with Abdi was raided. CAUGHT ON CAMERA: SQUAD DEM SQUIRMS WHEN PRESSED ON VANCE DOJ FRAUD PROBE Omar's son is not accused of any wrongdoing, nor is Omar, but the incident raised concerns over Hirsi's close affiliations. The congresswoman, meanwhile, refused to give her take on the latest controversy. "What do you know about the situation, why it happened in the first place?" Omar was asked as she walked through the halls of Capitol Hill. She ignored the inquiry and walked away but was hounded with more questions on the matter. "Are you going to advise your son to move from his place? Away from that situation? We were just wondering what you thought about the whole thing," she was pressed in follow-ups. FEDERAL APPEALS COURT UPHOLDS CONTROVERSIAL ILLINOIS BAN ON SEMIAUTOMATIC GUNS The Minnesota lawmaker, Somali refugee and first hijab-wearing woman elected to Congress, continued to walk in silence as she was peppered with questions. Omar's office did not immediately respond to a request from Fox News Digital. Abdi, who faces a weapons charge, was released the day after he was arrested. He was arrested 10 times in the past and has a felony speeding conviction stemming from an arrest in 2024 for driving more than 100 miles per hour. JD VANCE SAYS DOJ LOOKING INTO IF ILHAN OMAR COMMITTED IMMIGRATION FRAUD AMID BROTHER-MARRIAGE ALLEGATIONS Omar takes a strict stance on firearm regulation, advocating for the closure of the gun show loophole and the implementation of "red flag" laws to temporarily block individuals deemed a threat to public safety from accessing guns. She has also voted in support of legislation to prohibit the sale of assault-style weapons and to strengthen the universal background check system. "Not a good look for Ilhan Omar," Right-wing activist Benny Johnson wrote on X. articles.title: Trump on convention crowd booing Thune: ‘No, no. John is working hard’
articles.summary: President Trump on Wednesday told the crowd at the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) first midterm convention in Dallas not to boo the absent Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), telling them that “John is working hard.” Trump mentioned Thune’s name after he said Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) “will go down as the greatest Speaker of…
articles.body:
President Trump on Wednesday told the crowd at the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) first midterm convention in Dallas not to boo the absent Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), telling them that “John is working hard.”

Trump mentioned Thune’s name after he said Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) “will go down as the greatest Speaker of the House in the history of our country.” He then added, Thune was “here” before asking where he was, prompting boos from the audience.

“No, no. John is working hard. He’s got great opposition. He’s got great opposition from the Democrat –– Schumer and these guys, they’re terrible. Great opposition,” he continued, referring to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.). “He’s working very hard. He’s gonna have great success. You watch.”

The president added that Senate Republicans will in general have “great, great success.”

Thune and Trump have been at odds with each other as Thune has dismissed the chances of passing the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) America) Act, Trump’s priority legislation — which would require a photo ID when casting a ballot and proof of citizenship in order to register to vote.

Trump pressed the GOP leader to keep the Senate in session earlier this summer to get the bill passed rather than let senators go for recess, to no avail. The president has also called for an end to the filibuster, which Thune has ruled out of consideration without enough votes to do so.

The South Dakota Republican has also expressed his worry over the GOP maintaining their majority in the upper chamber of Congress, telling Keloland News earlier this month that he’s a “realist” and that the Senate is “a competitive environment right now.”

Trump has not endorsed Thune for another term in the Senate and suggested, while selling his administration’s successes, that Republican voters are not happy with current leadership and that they think he isn’t getting the job done. The president told Punchbowl News in an interview last month that he gets along with the senator, but said it was “unfortunate that he doesn’t have the votes.”

“I believe strongly in terminating the filibuster, and by the way, getting SAVE America Act approved immediately, and about 400 other things in every hour of every day,” he told the outlet.

Senate Republicans have rallied to support Thune, with Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.), a chief proponent of the SAVE America Act, saying that if he were president, “I would be frustrated if everything I wanted didn’t get done.”

“It’s a hard job, it’s really a hard job,” Scott previously told The Hill.
